The decibel is a kind of marine shellfish. It is edible and delicious, and belongs to the class Lamellibranchia (or Bivalvia) of the phylum Mollusca…

Whoa, whoa, hold on. Sorry, wrong channel: I seem to have wandered into a nature documentary. (In Chinese, the “bel” in decibel is written with the character for shellfish.)

The decibel we are talking about today has nothing to do with food. It is a unit of measurement. Most people know the word from acoustics, where it describes how loud a sound is, but the decibel is not limited to acoustics: it is also used in electrical engineering, optics and other fields.

Sound curiosities

First, to get a feel for decibels (rough estimates):

Breathing: 10 dB

Speaking softly: 30 dB

Rain: 50 dB

Restaurant: 70 dB

Concert: 80 dB

Power drill: 95 dB

Crowd at a ball game: 115 dB

Thunder: 120 dB

Gunshot: 140 dB

Rocket launch: 160 dB

A feel for decibels

When we say a sound is so many decibels, we usually take a point 1 m from the source as the reference. The values above are only rough estimates, because we don’t know where they were measured.

So what are the limits of sound in this world? Let’s see. (Again, we don’t know how far from the source these were measured, and the figures can’t be verified, so just enjoy the show -_-) [4]

The loudest aircraft: XF-84H

140 dB. Clearly audible 40 km away. 140 − 92 = 48 dB. Yep, as long as you’re not getting on in years, you should hear it.

The US military’s “Thunderscreech”

The Saturn V rocket

204 dB. From a beast with 7.5 million pounds of thrust.

NASA

The Soviet Tsar Bomba

224 dB. Reportedly more than 3,000 times as powerful as the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombs.

nationalinterest

Krakatoa, Indonesia

310 dB. Suppose this value was measured 1 m from the volcano as a sound source (whatever a volcano “sound source” is supposed to mean...). New York is 20,000 km away from the volcano, so people in Times Square (assuming Times Square had time-traveled back to 1883) would still have heard about 160 dB! Fortunately, on its journey the sound “crossed mountains and seas, and passed through seas of people,” to borrow a line from the Chinese pop song “The Ordinary Road.” After attenuation in the air, reflection, scattering, diffraction and the rest, there is no way it could deliver those 160 dB to New Yorkers’ ears as crisply as Guo Degang, the crosstalk comedian, delivers a punchline. But according to reports, it could be heard in New York. COVID may have left all of humanity thoroughly fucked up, but the Indonesians back then seem to have had it worse.

The Chicxulub impact

How many dB? Only the dinosaurs could tell us. The asteroid struck with two million times the energy of the Tsar Bomba and changed both the Earth’s rotation and its orbit.

So how exactly is the decibel defined, and how do we work out how loud the sound was for New Yorkers?

Defining the decibel

The decibel, dB for short. Not Deutsche Bahn, not Deutsche Bank, not database, but deciBel, named after Bell, the inventor of the telephone [1], and introduced by Bell Labs in 1924. The prefix deci- is the one that means a tenth, so 1 dB = 1/10 B. In acoustics, sound pressure level (SPL), sound intensity level (SIL) and sound power level (SWL) are all expressed in dB.

Put simply, a dB value expresses the ratio of two quantities on a logarithmic scale. Sound pressure level, for example, is the ratio of a sound pressure to a reference sound pressure, expressed logarithmically. But if what the ear hears directly is sound pressure, why not just use sound pressure? Why all this converting back and forth with logarithms?

And now, prepare to witness a miracle. Well, “witness” is a stretch: the ear is just one of the countless miracles of the human body, and they play out in all of us every day.

How does the ear tell high notes from low ones?

Why use dB?

In short: convenience.

Let’s start with sound pressure level. Take a time-varying sound signal in the time domain, p(t)

Its sound pressure level is strictly defined as

L=20log10(prms/p0) dB

where prms is the root mean square of the sound pressure over the stretch of signal being evaluated, calculated as

prms=1T∫0Tp2(t)dt

Broadly speaking, the sound pressure level represents the signal’s average magnitude. p0 is the reference sound pressure, p0=2×10−5Pa

This reference pressure represents the average threshold of human hearing, that is, the sound pressure of the quietest sound we can hear. The loudest sound we can hear is around 1000 Pa [2] (154 dB; at that level most people would probably be bleeding from every orifice), fifty million times the quietest! On the one hand, such an enormous range shows just how awesome the ear is, with superb sensitivity and dynamic range. On the other hand, it makes sound pressure a pain to express. Think of the Zimbabwe dollar a few years ago, when it took quadrillions to buy one US dollar: very inconvenient.

This is where that gangster of a tool, the logarithm, comes into its own. Let’s see what the sound pressures between the thresholds of hearing look like on a logarithmic scale.

Amazingly, sound pressures spanning nearly eight orders of magnitude (x-axis) are mapped onto 0–154 dB of sound pressure level (y-axis). On the right of the figure below, the x-axis has been switched to a logarithmic scale, and the relationship between sound pressure level and sound pressure becomes a straight line.

Sound pressure level vs. sound pressure. Left: linear axis; right: logarithmic axis

Note that sound pressure level does not fully and directly reflect how loud we perceive a sound to be [3]. That is why A-weighting exists. I covered A-weighting and loudness in my psychoacoustics articles.

We all know that sound pressure level in dB (decibels) is the agreed measure of how loud a sound is in acoustics. In psychoacoustics, though, there are people in the loop. Because the ear is insensitive to low frequencies, the low-frequency part is attenuated, giving the A-weighted sound pressure level, written dB(A) or dBA. I explained this in detail in my earlier article on psychoacoustics, so I won’t repeat it here.

A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 1

A-weighting curve [community.sw.siemens.com/]

A-weighting is easy to apply. Say the sound pressure level at 100 Hz is 100 dB. Look up the A-weighting curve: the attenuation at 100 Hz is 20 dB, so the A-weighted level is 100 − 20 = 80 dB(A).

1 + 1 ≠ 2

I once answered a question on Zhihu: if two pianos each play at 90 dB at the same time, is the result 180 dB? After my explanation above, I’m sure you already know the answer. If it were yes, two pianos would make an easy recipe for a sweet-sounding nuclear weapon bursting with energy.

Suppose we have two signals whose RMS sound pressures over the same time interval are p1 and p2, both with the same sound pressure level of 90 dB.

There are three cases to consider [2]:

in phase, in antiphase and incoherent. In-phase and antiphase signals are both coherent.

1. In phase, the two waveforms are exactly the same. Say two pianos play at the same time: the sound pressure level reaching the ear goes up by 6 dB. But +6 dB requires a whole list of assumptions: both pianos the same distance from the ear, both tuned identically, identical transmission paths for the direct and reflected sound of the fundamentals and harmonics, no binaural effects, and so on.

2. The extreme case (hard to achieve in practice): if the two signals are exactly opposite in phase, they interfere destructively at the ear and we hear nothing at all. This is why we have to treat a signal as something that varies in time, not just as an averaged sound pressure level.

3. Setting the original question aside, if the two signals are incoherent, the p1p2 term in Lsum can be neglected, and the result is +3 dB. Back to point 1: why did we need all those assumptions? Because in reality, the signals reaching the ear may well have become much less coherent.

Similar questions include:

If the sound pressure doubles, how much does the sound pressure level go up?

If the distance doubles, how much does the sound pressure level go down?

After the discussion above, that’s so easy. Mom never has to worry about my math again.

Double the sound pressure: up by 20log10(2)=6 dB;

Double the distance: p∼1/r, so doubling the distance halves the sound pressure: 20log10(1/2)=−6 dB, a drop of 6 dB in sound pressure level.

References

[1] Blauert, J., & Xiang, N. (2009). Acoustics for engineers: Troy lectures. Springer Science & Business Media.

[2] Vorländer, M. (2007). Auralization: fundamentals of acoustics, modelling, simulation, algorithms and acoustic virtual reality. Springer Science & Business Media.

[3] Kuttruff, H. (2007). Acoustics: an introduction. CRC Press.

[4] https://www.zmescience.com/science/the-loudest-sound-ever-in-mankinds-history/
